cells.tense: You are here with the pen, and what's finished is being let finish.
cells.act: trade one thing for one thing, and keep no score
cells.ask: Pick a swap with someone that has drifted out of kilter — you carrying more, or giving less than is fair. Say what each side puts in, out loud, then land on a single trade you can both keep from here.
cells.core:
A shared thing has done its work with you, and you can tell. A habit of feeling, a way you and another person have done it since before you can remember — when it's done, you release it, and you trust what comes after. The people close to you can feel that what you let go is let go cleanly, not dropped on them.

So work the next one aloud. Take an exchange that has drifted out of proportion and say what you're owed and what you owe in the same breath. Hear the other side. Land on a fair swap you can both keep, then stop counting. That is how the ends you make stop feeling like verdicts — they become trades, kept loosely, and the room after them is one nobody has to defend.
cells.sheetLine: You can let a shared thing end without it becoming a loss.
cells.verb: letting what is finished end, so what comes next can begin
cells.place: at the threshold where the old thing is done and the new one hasn't started

cells.tense: You'll be clearing the next thing before it has had a chance to live.
cells.act: sit with someone in it without fixing it
cells.ask: Choose a shared thing you're ready to end and stay inside it with whoever it still belongs to. Sit there, not above it, and let what it does for each of them reach you before you move to close it.
cells.core:
Something shared is being cut loose before it has lived. A group, a way you meet, a feeling you've decided is over — from where you stand it looks stale, and the clearing feels like air. From the far side it seems as though nothing is permitted to stay long enough to matter. People have started keeping from you the things they'd rather you didn't end.

What's missing is contact, not restraint — being inside what's still alive alongside the ones it belongs to. Because you can't clear well what you won't sit in. Stay in a shared thing you'd rather end, beside whoever it still belongs to, and feel what it's carrying for someone who isn't you. The endings you make afterward will be the right ones, and there will be fewer.
cells.sheetLine: You're clearing the table before anyone has eaten.
cells.verb: letting what is finished end, so what comes next can begin
cells.place: at the threshold where the old thing is done and the new one hasn't started

cells.tense: You were standing at a door that closed behind you a season ago.
cells.act: move toward the thing you want, one step, today
cells.ask: Take the smallest real step toward a direction that still pulls you — make the call, sign up, walk over — and take it before the day ends, while the old slot still sits on your calendar.
cells.core:
Something you cared about is over and you're still keeping its place warm. The date you go through, the habit you rehearse, the person you wait to hear from — the event has finished and you haven't finished attending it. That keeping is loyal, and it is quietly costing you the hours something alive would use.

You don't have to kill it. Move a wanted thing into the slot the finished one still occupies, and go there instead. One real step in a direction that still pulls you, taken today, before the old slot gets filled by another week of waiting. What's over ends by being replaced, not by being buried, and you don't owe anyone an announcement. Doors close when you simply walk through a different one.
cells.sheetLine: It's over. You've been going on keeping it.
cells.verb: letting what is finished end, so what comes next can begin
cells.place: at the threshold where the old thing is done and the new one hasn't started

cells.tense: Something is already ending by your own hand while you tell yourself nothing is.
cells.act: put a date, a place, a container on it
cells.ask: Put a date on the day you'll stop keeping the old way going. Write it in a calendar only you open — not a speech, not shared with anyone — and hold to it. A thinning with an edge is something you can stand behind.
cells.core:
Something between you and the people near you is already ending — the shape of your gatherings, a story you tell about yourself, a habit of feeling that has gone quiet. You are the one letting it end, gently, by not renewing it. Ask you and you'd say nothing was happening. It is, and your hand is on the pen.

Give it an edge. The old way is thinning so slowly that nobody, including you, can point to it. Put a date in a calendar only you open for the day you'll stop keeping it going, and hold to that. It doesn't need announcing. The others can already feel something shifting — a date just gives the shift a shape, and puts the shape in your hand instead of in the air.
cells.sheetLine: Something shared is ending, by your hand, unsigned.
cells.verb: letting what is finished end, so what comes next can begin
cells.place: at the threshold where the old thing is done and the new one hasn't started

attempts.check: The unsupported claim: in the Balanced cell I read 'an old bond, a role you took on, a season of feeling' as things some shared exchange is out of proportion around — the record gives only the general mechanism (give and receive out of balance, Structure channel), never which exchange or who. A reader could object that nothing between them and anyone else is off, that the endings with a date are private. The ask still survives that: put the owed thing and the owed-to-you thing on one page is useful even if the imbalance is entirely internal, because it's a practice of calibration, not a verdict about anyone. The sentence that serves me more than them: 'let the feeling finish before you call the share fair' — it sounds wise, but it edits their speed without their consent; cut it to a concrete action.
